title: Redwood discovery - reliability & multi-region fallbacks with Aurora Enterprises
summary: Initial discovery focused on Aurora's reliability needs for customer-facing LLM features. Customer runs in AWS across us-east-1/us-west-2 and wants predictable latency plus graceful degradation during incidents. Key questions: hosted vs dedicated vs private tradeoffs, multi-region routing and automatic failover, SLA expectations, audit logs and KMS, and POC benchmarking. Redwood AE/SE proposed a dedicated pilot with multi-tier fallback policies (model variants, region failover, and degraded-response modes) and agreed to share security docs, pricing, and a benchmark plan.
next_steps: Samir to send Dedicated pricing + example contract (by 2027-03-03)
Maya to share security whitepaper and SOC2 artifacts link (by 2027-03-02)
Aurora to provide sample traffic profile and critical endpoints for benchmarking (by 2027-03-05)
Run an initial latency and failover benchmark during POC
action_items: Samir Patel - Send Dedicated pricing, example contract, and canary rollout playbook - 2027-03-03
Maya Chen - Share security docs (SOC2, ISO summary), KMS integration notes, and SAML SSO guide - 2027-03-02

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-02-28
Start: 15:00 UTC
Duration: ~48 minutes
Attendees: Samir Patel (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (CTO, Aurora), Rashida Khan (Head of Platform), Jon Park (SRE)
Recording id: ff-20270228-aurora-001

[00:00:00] Samir: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Samir, AE on the Redwood side, with Maya our SE. How's everybody doing?
[00:00:08] Liam: Hey Samir, good thanks. Excited to dig into reliability stuff. We're looking at Redwood for some customer-facing features so uptime is a big deal.
[00:00:18] Rashida: Yeah hi all, we run most services in AWS across us-east-1 and us-west-2, and want multi-region failover for LLM scenarios.
[00:00:26] Maya: Great, that's exactly the sort of thing we've been helping similar customers with. Quick agenda: understand your constraints, talk Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs for incident tolerance, routing/fallback policies, SLAs, and then next steps for a POC. Sound OK?
[00:00:38] Jon: Yep. Also want to dig into KMS and audit logs — we have compliance needs.
[00:00:43] Samir: Perfect. Liam can you give a bit of background on the product surface where you're planning to use models and what your SLOs are?
[00:00:52] Liam: Sure. Two primary flows: realtime chat support assistant (low latency target <=120ms p50) and async summarization for transcripts where latency can be higher. We do about 800 rps at peak for the chat endpoints, 2 replicas per region now. SLOs are 99.9% for chat; we can't have minute-plus outages.
[00:01:13] Rashida: To be clear, 99.9% across our userbase, and we need predictable tail latency. Cost matters but we won't accept consistency tradeoffs that break UX.
[00:01:22] Maya: Understood. A couple clarifying q's: do you need single-digit ms routing between regions, or is cross-region warm standby OK? Also are you open to Dedicated reserved pools for predictable capacity?
[00:01:33] Liam: We want active-active if feasible, but active-passive with sub-500ms failover would be acceptable. We're open to Dedicated if it gives predictable throughput — but we'll evaluate cost. Private (VPC/on-prem) is only if required for compliance.
[00:01:48] Samir: Okay. At a high level: Hosted is our managed offering, we run the model in our regions and provide routing. For customers with strict SLOs, Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity in the region(s) you choose, lower variance and predictable throughput. Private moves the control plane into your VPC or on-prem and is for regulated workloads. In terms of incident tolerance, we layer policies: region routing, model fallbacks, and degraded-response modes (e.g., shorter context, smaller model) — those are pluggable.
[00:02:16] Jon: Can you walk through a concrete failover example? Say us-east-1 has an outage.
[00:02:21] Maya: Sure. Typical policy: 1) health probes from our control plane detect region outage; 2) smart routing redirects traffic to us-west-2 (or another region) with connection draining; 3) if Dedicated capacity is limited in the failover region, we automatically fall back to a lighter model variant — for example from redwood-xxl to redwood-large with reduced token budgets — that preserves semantics but reduces compute. We also have an option to send a degraded response with cached prefix completions for critical routes.
[00:02:50] Liam: That sounds promising. How fast is the detection and cutover? We need to measure RTO.
[00:02:55] Maya: Health detection is configurable; typically probes are 5–15s and routing changes propagate in under 60s for standard setups. With Dedicated and routing preconfigured (sticky DNS + anycast + our edge), we can get cutover down to ~20–30s in many cases. But there are network and cold-start caveats.
[00:03:13] Rashida: Cold start meaning model warmup? We can't have a 30s spike in latency for customers.
[00:03:18] Maya: Correct — to manage that we recommend warm standby pools, KV cache prewarming, and graceful degradation paths. If you reserve Dedicated capacity in both regions we can keep models hot and reduce cold starts. There's a cost tradeoff.
[00:03:30] Jon: What's the recommended configuration if we want p50 <=120ms and 99.9% availability?
[00:03:36] Samir: For that SLO we'd propose Dedicated in primary and failover regions with autoscaling buffers, plus our multi-region routing enabled. Also configure fallback policies to lower model size at the 95th/99th percentile to preserve throughput. We'll propose numbers in the POC.
[00:03:50] Liam: SLA — what does Redwood guarantee for Hosted vs Dedicated?
[00:03:54] Maya: Hosted has our standard SLA (99.5% uptime for API endpoints on the hosted tier). Dedicated comes with stronger SLAs depending on commitment — we offer 99.9%+ with reserved pools and support SLAs in the contract. Private is negotiable as part of enterprise licensing. I'll attach the SLA matrix.
[00:04:10] Rashida: Good. Also need to know how SLO breaches are measured — token latency vs end-to-end user latency.
[00:04:16] Maya: We can provide both token-level metrics and end-to-end request latency in the Console dashboards and traces. We recommend defining user-facing SLOs at the request level, but we can instrument both.
[00:04:25] Liam: On security — KMS integration and audit logs are mandatory for us. How do you handle customer-managed keys and logs retention?
[00:04:32] Maya: We support customer-managed keys via KMS/HSM integrations for Private and Dedicated. For Hosted we offer envelope encryption with optional customer-provided keys in some regions. Audit logs and per-request traces are available; longer retention is an add-on. We'll share SOC2 docs and a KMS integration guide.
[00:04:49] Jon: Network setup: if we do Private in a VPC, what's the egress/ingress pattern? We need to avoid opening broad outbound rules.
[00:04:57] Samir: Private deployments can be configured with narrow egress rules and private endpoints. For Dedicated we use secure peering and can limit egress to specific IP ranges; we'll provide the minimal port list.
[00:05:06] Rashida: Are there known cases where fallback to smaller models changed response quality significantly? We need to understand tradeoffs.
[00:05:12] Maya: In our experience, semantic fidelity remains good in most prompt types when moving from xxl->large for extractive tasks, but creative/long-context coherence can degrade. That's why we run quality guards and A/B evals during POC. Also recommend progressive degradation: reduce context length, then model size, then sampling temperature to keep helpful output while saving compute.
[00:05:33] Liam: For POC, what benchmarks will you run?
[00:05:36] Maya: We'll run latency (p50/p95/p99), throughput under load, failover RTO/RPO simulations, and quality regression tests on a sample prompt set you provide. We'll simulate region outage and also saturate Dedicated capacity to trigger fallback policies.
[00:05:50] Jon: How do you handle KV cache and prefix caching across regions? If cache is region-local, failover can lose warm state.
[00:05:59] Maya: Good point. KV cache is typically per-region; we do offer shared cache replication in some Dedicated setups, but that's an advanced config. Common approach: we keep small warm standby caches in failover regions or keep cacheable prefixes on the client so they can be replayed. We'll outline options in the POC plan.
[00:06:18] Liam: Are there telemetry hooks we can integrate into our monitoring? Prometheus metrics, traces?
[00:06:22] Maya: Yes we expose metrics endpoints and tracing hooks; Console has tracing that can export traces. For Dedicated we can also push metrics into your Prometheus/CloudWatch.
[00:06:30] Rashida: Cost question: if we run Dedicated in two regions with warm standby, how much overhead should we expect?
[00:06:37] Samir: Rough rule of thumb: warm standby in a second region is 25–40% of primary capacity cost if machines are right-sized and autoscaling is tuned. We'll put exact estimates in the pricing.
[00:06:48] Liam: Competitors we've looked at: Anthropic and AWS Bedrock. Both have different strengths but we're leaning toward Redwood for the operational controls.
[00:06:56] Maya: Thanks. We also integrate with existing infra patterns — nothing exotic.
[00:07:02] [00:07:02] Jon: Quick clarification, you mentioned degraded-response mode — can you give an example response that indicates graceful degradation?
[00:07:07] Maya: Example: if user asks for a long-form summary and model falls back, we return a shorter summary and a note like "Condensed result due to system load; full summary available later" along with a request id. That allows the client to surface a user-friendly message.
[00:07:20] Liam: Nice. On observability, will we get per-request IDs to correlate with our logs?
[00:07:24] Maya: Yes each request includes a request id and trace id. We'll give you mapping of fields.
[00:07:29] Rashida: Anything from our side to prepare for the POC?
[00:07:33] Samir: We'll need sample traffic, list of critical endpoints, SAML metadata if you want SSO, and networking details for the VPC if you want Private. Also define success criteria for the POC — e.g., p95 < X ms during failover test and quality within Y% of baseline.
[00:07:49] Liam: We'll put together the sample traffic and success criteria. One ask: can you share an example canary rollout and automatic fallback policy config?
[00:07:57] Maya: Yes I'll attach a playbook. Our typical canary is traffic split 5/95 for 24–48 hours with auto rollback on error rates or quality regressions. Fallback policies are a priority-ordered list: region -> model variant -> degraded response.
[00:08:12] Jon: How do you measure quality regressions automatically? We need to avoid subtle semantic drift.
[00:08:16] Maya: We run evals against a labeled test set and compute metrics like BLEU/ROUGE for extractive tasks and embedding similarity/regression alerts for semantic tasks. We can also run a small human-in-the-loop sample during canaries.
[00:08:30] Liam: Any gotchas with DNS TTL during failover? We use low TTL but want to avoid flapping.
[00:08:34] Maya: We use a combination of edge routing and short TTLs. To avoid flapping we incorporate hysteresis and backoff in our routing rules.
[00:08:42] Rashida: For contract/legal: do you provide liability limits in the SLA for Dedicated?
[00:08:46] Samir: Yes liability and SLA credits are part of the enterprise contract. We'll have legal and our pricing team draft the terms.
[00:08:53] Liam: Ok, would you be able to run an initial failover sim next week as a demo?
[00:08:58] Maya: We can schedule a run during the POC kick-off; it'll be a controlled simulation where we fail a region and measure RTO/RPO.
[00:09:05] [00:09:05] Rashida: Are there examples of customers who've done active-active with you at our scale?
[00:09:10] Maya: Yes — a payments customer at similar RPS runs Dedicated active-active across us-east/us-west with autoscaling buffers and saw sub-100ms p50 and RTO ~25s using warm standby. I'll anonymize and share the benchmarking spreadsheet.
[00:09:22] Jon: For encryption at rest with customer keys — do you support key rotation without downtime?
[00:09:28] Maya: We support key rotation via KMS with rolling re-encryption; if configured correctly rotation is online. We'll provide the ops steps.
[00:09:36] Liam: Any limitations on private deployments in terms of feature parity?
[00:09:40] Samir: Feature parity is high; a few managed analytics features may require managed Console connectivity. In Private we can offer audit log export and most features but some managed telemetry endpoints are optional.
[00:09:51] [00:09:51] Rashida: Great. Let's talk timeline: we're aiming for production rollout in Q2 if POC goes well. Are you resourced for that?
[00:09:58] Samir: Yes our typical engagement for Dedicated POCs is 4–6 weeks for benchmarking and initial rollout; Private takes longer depending on networking. We'll prioritize this if you move forward.
[00:10:08] Liam: Perfect. Any immediate risks we should be aware of?
[00:10:12] Maya: Main risks are cost for warm standby, complexity around cache warmups across regions, and ensuring PII/data residency if you have strict requirements. We'll surface mitigations in the POC doc.
[00:10:24] Samir: Quick recap of agreed items: Redwood to send Dedicated pricing + contract, security docs, POC plan with benchmark matrix, Aurora to send sample traffic and routes, schedule POC kick-off.
[00:10:36] Liam: Sounds good.
[00:10:38] Rashida: We'll aim to get the artifacts to you by Friday.
[00:10:41] Samir: Great. Any other questions?
[00:10:44] Jon: One more: how do you handle rate-limiting during overload? Do you return 429 or queue?
[00:10:49] Maya: We support multiple policies: 429 with retry-after, queued requests with best-effort if latency budgets allow, and backpressure that triggers fallbacks. Configurable per route.
[00:10:59] Liam: That's useful. Ok thanks everyone. Let's wrap.
[00:11:03] Samir: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the docs and proposed dates.

Notes / Artifacts referenced:
- Redwood Dedicated pricing (link to be sent)
- Redwood security whitepaper & SOC2 (link: https://redwood.ai/security)
- Example canary playbook (will attach)
- Benchmarking spreadsheet (will share during POC)

End of recording.
